Read from the briefing site (source: TUM.ai's open-sourced scoring platform). Every submitted repo
gets a six-stage AI review on GitHub Actions after the Sun 2026-08-23 12:00 deadline; judges see the
report cards before ranking ordinally.

Weighted dimensions (1–10 each): code quality 30 · architecture 25 · challenge alignment 25 ·

- **Boilerplate ratio 0.3–0.5.** Untouched generator output reads ~0.9. Delete unused scaffolding,
  default logos, example tests, dead code — scaffold heavily, then strip hard.
- **Git activity must read `normal`:** commit roughly every 30 min with a real message. Avoid
  `single_large_commit` and `minimal_history`.
- **Echo the brief's exact phrases** (once it drops at 10:00) in README, headings, commit messages —
  the sponsor's brief text is pasted into the grader's prompt.
- **Prompt/process score** (advisory, jury-read): ownership_language 35, technical_specificity 25,
  iteration_verification 25, edge_case_awareness 15. Write prompts stating my own reasoning and
  rejected alternatives, not bare commands.
- AI authorship is explicitly NOT penalised, so no reason to hide agent use.
- Ship something: any submission +2, no submission 0. Freeze scope early.

## What it is, in plain terms

QuantCo works on **P&C insurance claims** — property & casualty, i.e. "my pipe burst and wrecked the floor" claims. Today a human claim handler reads the description, looks at photos and a repair invoice, and decides whether the price is fair. That's slow, and the experienced handlers are retiring.

**The challenge is a game, not a normal build.** Every team plays two roles at once:

**Role 1 — Issuer (you're the repair company sending a bill).**
You get a damage case and set a **charge price `a`**. You want it as high as possible, but every case has a **hidden fair value `t`**. Price under `t` = fair, and you get paid. Price over `t` = that's fraud, and you get caught.

**Role 2 — Insurance (you're paying other teams' bills).**
You set an **acceptance limit `b`** — the most you'll pay for that same line item. Too high and you overpay for someone's inflated invoice. Too low and you reject a legitimate claim — and the slides say if you decline and your limit was below what the experts consider fair, you eat the **payout plus a penalty**. So being paranoid is punished too.

## How a round works

- A new case drops **every 10 minutes**: a damage description, a `policy.txt`, an invoice, sometimes a photo.
- You get **1 minute** to analyze it and submit your two numbers, `a` and `b`.
- You play against **every other team** simultaneously — you're billing them, they're billing you.
- Scoring is `income − costs = net`, shown on a live leaderboard. The example shows most teams sitting at negative net (they paid out and earned nothing), so the leaders are the ones who both priced sharply *and* rejected the overpriced bills.

## What this actually means for us

The one-minute window is the whole point. You can't read a PDF invoice, check it against a policy, and estimate a fair German repair cost by hand in 60 seconds — **you need an agent pipeline that ingests the case files and outputs `a` and `b`**. That's the real deliverable.

I read the deck plus the pre-event dossier at `/Users/pavinsp/Desktop/EHL HACKATHON/quantco.md`. The handout the slides mention isn't anywhere on disk — so everything below comes from the 6 slides. Numbers in my example are made up to show the mechanics.

## The setting

QuantCo does **P&C insurance** — property & casualty. Burst pipes, hail damage, a flooded floor. Someone repairs the damage, sends an invoice, the insurer decides whether to pay.

The hard part is that the invoice is just a PDF written by a repair firm. Was €40/m² for new laminate fair, or did they pad it? A human claim handler answers that from experience. Those handlers are retiring, and slide 2 says Germany alone pays out **>€55 billion a year** in retail insurance.

## The game

Every case has a **hidden fair value `t`** — what QuantCo's experts say the work is really worth. You never see it. You play both sides of every case:

**As the Issuer** you send the bill. You pick a **charge price `a`**.
- `a` below `t` → fair invoice, and whoever accepts it pays you.
- `a` above `t` → that's fraud. It gets rejected and you earn nothing.
- So you want `a` just *barely* under `t`. Greedy but not caught.

**As the Insurance** you receive other teams' bills. You pick an **acceptance limit `b`** — the most you'll pay for that same line item.
- Bill comes in at or under `b` → you pay it.
- Bill comes in above `b` → you decline.
- **But**: if you decline something the experts consider fair, you pay the **payout plus a penalty**. Being trigger-happy is punished.

Both numbers, same case, same one-minute window.

## A worked example

The case on slide 5: *"The water pipe in the living room broke..."* You get the damage description, a `policy.txt`, an invoice, and sometimes a photo. The invoice lines up as:

| # | Line item | Qty | Hidden fair unit price | Hidden fair `t` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Remove water-damaged laminate | 18 m² | €10/m² | €180 |
| 2 | New laminate incl. impact sound insulation | 18 m² | €40/m² | €720 |
| 3 | Replace skirting boards | 25 lfm | €10/lfm | €250 |

Take line 2, fair value **€720**. Now four outcomes:

**You issue at `a` = €690** → under €720, fair. Any team whose limit is ≥ €690 pays you. **You earn €690.** You left €30 on the table, but you got paid.

**You issue at `a` = €950** → over €720, that's fraud. Teams with a sane limit reject it. **You earn €0** on that line. Your greed cost you the whole €720 you could have banked.

**You're the insurer, limit `b` = €800**, and a rival bills €950. You decline. Your limit was above the fair €720, so the decline was justified — **you pay nothing.** Good call.

**You're the insurer, limit `b` = €600**, and a rival bills €690 — which was fair. You decline it anyway. Your limit sat *below* fair value, so **you pay the €690 anyway, plus a penalty.** This is the worst square on the board, and it's the trap. Paranoid insurers lose money.

Notice the shape of it: if you knew `t` exactly you'd set `a` = €719 and `b` = €721 and print money. **Every euro of uncertainty in your estimate costs you real money** — you have to drop `a` to stay safe and raise `b` to avoid the penalty. That gap is your ignorance, priced.

## How a round runs

- New case drops **every 10 minutes**.
- **1 minute** to read it and submit your `a` and `b`.
- You face **every other team at once** — billing them, being billed by them.
- Live leaderboard, ranked by **net = income − costs**.

## What the leaderboard on slide 6 is telling us

Look at the example standings:

| Rank | Team | Income | Costs | Net |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Ingenious Inigo | 7087.50 | 802.24 | **+6285.26** |
| 2 | Hammer Hannes | 3737.10 | 2058.75 | +1678.35 |
| 3–6 | four teams | **0.00** | ~2750–3247 | −2750 to −3247 |

The bottom four earned **literally nothing** — every invoice they issued was priced above fair and got rejected. And three of them have *identical* costs of 3247.38, which means they all accepted everything thrown at them. Overpriced and overpaid, both sides wrong.

The winner did both jobs well: high income (priced just under fair) *and* costs of only €802 (caught the padded bills). You can't win on one side alone.

## What we'd actually have to build

Sixty seconds. You cannot open a PDF, cross-check a policy document, and estimate German laminate rates by hand in that time. So the deliverable is a pipeline that:

1. Parses the invoice into line items with quantity and unit,
2. Reads `policy.txt` to check what's even covered,
3. Estimates a fair unit price per line item,
4. Optionally reads the photo to sanity-check the claim ("this room is not 18 m²"),
5. Emits `a` and `b` with a safety margin driven by its own confidence,
6. Learns from previous rounds — the leaderboard has **Transactions / Matchup / All Games** tabs, which is feedback we can calibrate against.

Slide 6 also says **"Your methodology also counts (style!)"**, so the leaderboard isn't the whole score. That matches the EHL rubric in my memory — code quality 30, architecture 25.

## What we still don't know

The slides promise a handout, and it isn't in Downloads. Three things in it will change the design:

- **How big is the penalty?** It decides how much padding `b` needs. That's the single most important number in the game.
- **Is `t` per line item or per invoice total?** Slide 5 says `b` applies to "the same line item", so probably per item — but that changes the whole data model.
- **Does VAT count?** The invoice has Net / plus VAT / Total. Charging on the wrong one is a ~19% error, which is more than most teams' margin.

Want me to go after the handout, or start sketching the pipeline against what we know?

Two things changed from the PDF, and one matters for design: rounds are **15 minutes**, not 10, and each round gives you a **blank invoice** — you author the line items yourself, rather than auditing a pre-filled one as the slide showed.

Also urgent: **team check-in is 4 of 5**, and you can't register for any challenge until all five are in. Deadline is 13:30 CET, ~1h55m out. Chase that now, before the decision.

## My pick: Viktor's Router

It's the only one of the three where you're handed a dataset and can finish offline. Nothing depends on credits you don't have, no live opponents, no overnight babysitting. All three judged criteria — accuracy, evaluation, generality — are entirely under your control, and you can hold a held-out split back from hour one to make "generality" a number rather than a claim.

It also parallelizes cleanly across five people: data exploration, feature/embedding pipeline, the router itself, the eval harness, the deck. Everyone has work by 13:00.

The catch is that it's the most crowded pick — every ML-leaning team will reach for embeddings plus a classifier. You don't win it with the model, you win it with the evaluation. "Your own numbers, produced by a method someone else could rerun" and "be ready to defend both the number and the method" is the judges telling you exactly where the points are. Budget real time for a reproducible eval script and an honest baseline table, including the dumb baselines (always-biggest-model, random, cost-only).

## Why not the other two

**Cognition** is the highest ceiling and the worst fit for 24 hours. The bar is brutal: full autonomy with nobody in the middle, self-verification, and explicitly *not* one prepared example. On top of that you'd be building on Devin credits you haven't secured yet — that's still an open item in `notes.md` — and Devin sessions run in minutes, so your iteration loop is slower than the hackathon can absorb. Picking the industry alone will eat two hours of argument.

**QuantCo** is the fun one and genuinely has an edge available: all results are public afterwards, so a team that models opponents' acceptance limits across rounds can beat teams that just estimate fair value. But your score depends on who else showed up, "the more rounds it plays cleanly, the better" means someone is awake feeding it all night, and you're exposed to platform problems you don't control.

## What would flip me to QuantCo

If someone on the team genuinely wants the game-theory problem and you'll commit a person to round ops overnight — take it. The score is objective, so you can place well without a polished pitch, and the opponent-modeling angle is a real moat that most teams won't build. That's an upside play. Viktor is the expected-value play.

Given you're five people with a working setup and 24 hours, I'd take the expected-value play.

Regardless of which you choose: ask Cognition for the Devin credits anyway, and get the fifth check-in done in the next few minutes.

# Insurance Invoice Poker — QuantCo challenge brief

Team Bayern CodeWerk · EHL Munich (match 3) · 22–23 August 2026

This is our working reference for the challenge we selected. It records what the brief actually
says, what we have inferred from it, and the strategy and architecture we derived. Anything marked
**[C]** is confirmed from source material; **[I]** is our own reasoning; **[?]** is unverified and
needs checking against the handout or the live platform.

Sources:

- `~/Downloads/QuantCo Claim-to-Fame slides.pdf` — 6-slide deck handed out at the opening ceremony.
- The EHL challenge-selection page (ehl.gg, Munich match 3), which carries the official brief text
  and judging criteria.
- A handout referenced on slide 5 (*"More details can be found on our handout!"*) that we do
  **not** have yet. Several open questions below depend on it.

---

## 1. At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Official title | **Insurance Invoice Poker**, by QuantCo |
| Format | Leaderboard game played live against every other team |
| Round cadence | New case every **15 minutes** |
| Decision window | **1 minute** to analyse and submit |
| Prize | **€1000**, plus AirPods Pro 3 + €100 coding-agent credit per person |
| Submission deadline | Sunday 2026-08-23, 12:00 |
| Required deliverables | Pitch deck · GitHub repository · live demo |

Official one-liner: *"Bill high, pay low. Best margin wins."*

---

## 2. The domain

QuantCo works on **P&C insurance** — property and casualty. Burst pipes, hail damage, water on a
living-room floor. The business runs on a quiet negotiation: a tradesperson writes an invoice, an
insurer decides what it is really worth, and both sides are guessing what the other will accept.

Why it matters, from the deck **[C]**:

- Retail insurance payout in Germany alone is **over €55 billion a year**.
- Natural catastrophes are getting more frequent.
- Many claim handlers are retiring and few young people enter the vocation.

What makes it hard **[C]**: the data is mostly unstructured, a claim can stay open a long time and
accumulate more of it, decisions are made live, the diversity of what can happen in a claim is
enormous, and there is very little automation today.

The claims pipeline QuantCo showed: **Claim Data Intake** (telephone, documents, first notice of
loss, follow-up questions) → **Claim Assessment** (plausibility and coverage check, fraud and
recourse detection, cost estimation) → **Claim Settlement** (send experts, check invoices, make
payments).

---

## 3. The game

Every case has a **hidden fair value `t`** — what QuantCo's experts say the work is genuinely
worth. We never see it. Each team plays both sides of every case at once.

### Role 1 — Issuer

You are the tradesperson sending the bill. You set a **charge price `a`**, the amount you charge
opposing teams. The slide frames it as: *"How high can you price without crossing `t`?"*

- `a` below `t` → the invoice is fair, and any team whose limit clears it pays you.
- `a` above `t` → that is fraud. It gets rejected and you earn nothing on that item.

### Role 2 — Insurance

You are the insurer receiving other teams' bills. You set an **acceptance limit `b`**, the maximum
your team is willing to accept and pay when receiving the same line item from another team. The
slide frames it as: *"How low can you go without rejecting fair claims?"*

- Incoming bill at or under `b` → you pay it.
- Incoming bill above `b` → you decline.
- **Penalty rule [C]:** if you decline and your acceptance limit is below expert-accepted prices,
  you pay the **payout plus a penalty**.

### The round loop

Each round delivers a **new policy, a new damage report, and a blank invoice**. You author the line
items, set `a` and `b`, and submit inside the one-minute window. You face every other team
simultaneously — billing them while they bill you. Results are public afterwards.

Scoring is **net = income − costs**, shown on a live leaderboard.

---

## 4. Worked example

Using the case shown on slide 5: *"The water pipe in the living room broke, resulting in a…"*
Fair values here are invented to illustrate the mechanics — the real ones are hidden.

| # | Line item | Qty | Assumed fair unit price | Assumed fair `t` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Remove water-damaged laminate in living room | 18 m² | €10/m² | €180 |
| 2 | New laminate incl. impact sound insulation | 18 m² | €40/m² | €720 |
| 3 | Replace skirting boards | 25 lfm | €10/lfm | €250 |

Take line 2, fair value **€720**. Four outcomes:

**Issue at `a` = €690.** Under fair. Any team with a limit at or above €690 pays. **You earn €690.**
You left €30 on the table and got paid for the rest.

**Issue at `a` = €950.** Over fair — fraud. Sane opponents reject it. **You earn €0.** Greed cost
you the entire €720 you could have banked.

**Insure with `b` = €800**, rival bills €950. You decline. Your limit sat above the fair €720, so
the decline was justified and **you pay nothing.** Correct call.

**Insure with `b` = €600**, rival bills a fair €690. You decline anyway. Your limit was *below* fair
value, so **you pay the €690 plus a penalty.** This is the worst square on the board.

### The shape of the problem

If you knew `t` exactly you would set `a` = €719 and `b` = €721 and print money. You do not, so you
drop `a` to stay clear of fraud and raise `b` to stay clear of the penalty. **That spread is your
uncertainty, and you pay for it every round.**

---

## 5. Reading the sample leaderboard

Slide 6 shows an example standings table. It is demo data, but the shape is instructive:

| Rank | Team | Income | Costs | Net |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Ingenious Inigo | 7087.50 | 802.24 | **+6285.26** |
| 2 | Hammer Hannes | 3737.10 | 2058.75 | +1678.35 |
| 3 | Babo Bernhard | 0.00 | 2749.92 | −2749.92 |
| 4–6 | Turbo Tim, Fire Florian, Magic Marlene | 0.00 | 3247.38 | −3247.38 |

Two things fall out of this **[I]**:

- The bottom four earned **literally nothing**. Every invoice they issued was priced above fair and
  rejected. Overpricing is not a small penalty — it zeroes your income.
- Three of them share an **identical cost of 3247.38**, which means they accepted exactly the same
  set of incoming bills. That is the signature of default or wide-open limits.

The winner did both jobs: income of €7087 (priced just under fair) *and* costs of only €802 (caught
the padded bills). **You cannot win on one side alone.**

---

## 6. What we can see, and what we can infer

Confirmed **[C]**: *"You check other team's prices, they check yours"* (slide 4) and *"all results
are public afterwards"* (challenge page). The leaderboard has tabs for **Standings, Performance,
Games, Matchup, Transactions, All Games**.

Unconfirmed **[?]**: whether Transactions exposes raw `a` and `b` per team per line item or only
resulting payments, and whether the hidden fair value `t` is ever revealed after a round. Assume it
is not.

### Bounding `t` without being told it [I]

Every outcome constrains the hidden value. This is the core of our calibration loop:

- Bill €690, accepted → **`t` ≥ 690**
- Bill €950, rejected → **`t` < 950**
- Rival bills €820 and gets paid → **`t` ≥ 820**
- Decline at `b` = 600 and eat a penalty → **`t` > 600** (an expensive way to learn it)

After a few rounds on similar line items, the fair rate for "lay laminate, per m²" is squeezed into
a tight interval that nobody ever told us.

The same logic reads opponents: if Team X paid our €690 bill, then **`b_X` ≥ 690**. Tracked across
rounds, that tells us who is loose and who is tight, and therefore how high `a` can safely go.

**Probing asymmetry [I]:** probe with `a`, not `b`. A rejected invoice just earns nothing that
round. A wrong decline costs payout plus penalty. So be adventurous on the pricing side and
conservative on the acceptance side until the data is in.

---

## 7. Strategy

### The central claim

The penalty rule forces every rational team to keep `b` at or just above their own estimate of `t`,
because sitting below it is actively punished. If everyone's `b` hovers near fair value, then `a`
just under `t` gets paid by almost everyone. **The game therefore collapses to estimating `t`
accurately.** Opponent modelling is a real but second-order edge.

### The lever most teams will miss [I]

The invoice arrives **blank** — we author the line items — and the acceptance limit is defined per
**line item**, not per invoice total.

If that holds, adding a *legitimate* line item that other teams forget is nearly free revenue.
Water damage to a floor is not only "remove laminate, lay laminate": there is debris disposal,
furniture moving, drying-equipment rental, skirting boards. Each is judged separately against fair
value, so a **complete** invoice earns more than a **padded** one, without ever crossing into fraud.

Most teams will tune unit prices and never touch invoice completeness.

**This must be verified before we build on it.** If rejection turns out to be per invoice rather
than per line item, adding items becomes a risk instead of an edge. See open question 2.

### Consistency is an engineering problem, not a modelling one

The judging criteria include *"Consistency: the more rounds it plays cleanly, the better."* A bot
that plays every round through the night beats a smarter one that someone forgets to run at 03:00.
Build for unattended uptime: retries, timeouts, and a safe fallback bid on any failure path.

---

## 8. Architecture

```
fetch round → parse policy + damage report → build line items
           → estimate fair value per item (+ confidence interval)
           → a = t̂_low · (1 − margin),  b = t̂_high · (1 + margin)
           → submit → ingest public results → recalibrate
```

Stages:

1. **Ingest** — fetch the round's policy, damage report, and blank invoice.
2. **Understand** — extract damage type, affected areas, quantities, and the policy's coverage,
   deductible, and limits into a structured claim object.
3. **Compose** — build the line items, aiming for completeness against the damage described.
4. **Price** — quantity × unit rate from a German trade-rate knowledge base, producing a fair-value
   estimate and a confidence interval per line.
5. **Bid** — derive `a` and `b` from the interval, with the margin driven by confidence and by the
   penalty asymmetry.
6. **Submit** — inside the one-minute window, with a fallback bid if anything upstream fails.
7. **Learn** — ingest public results, tighten the rate intervals, and update per-opponent limit
   estimates.

Step 7 is the differentiator. It also answers two judged criteria directly: *"Generality: also works
on completely new policies"* and *"Approach: the strategy you went in with, and how it changed as
you played."*

---

## 9. Judging criteria (verbatim)

**What you built:**

- **Score** — Where you finished. The main signal, not the only one
- **Generality** — Also works on completely new policies
- **Consistency** — The more rounds it plays cleanly, the better

**How you pitch it:**

- **Clarity** — If we can't follow it, we can't credit it
- **Problem** — What's hard about pricing a claim from both sides
- **Approach** — The strategy you went in with, and how it changed as you played
- **Solution** — What you ended up with, and the logic behind it

Slide 6 adds: *"Your methodology also counts (style!)"*.

---

## 10. Work split

| Who | Owns |
|---|---|
| 1 | Platform integration, round loop, submission reliability |
| 2 | Policy and damage-report parsing → structured claim |
| 3 | German trade-rate knowledge base + fair-value estimator |
| 4 | Results ingestion, calibration, opponent modelling |
| 5 | Pitch deck, live demo, README and repo hygiene |

Slot 5 is not filler. The pitch carries half the rubric, and EHL's automated review extracts
`has_readme`, `has_dockerfile`, and `has_tests` mechanically and hands them to graders.

---

## 11. Open questions

Blocking or design-changing, in priority order:

1. **How large is the penalty for a wrong decline?** It sets the entire margin on `b`, and it is the
   single most important number in the game. **[?]**
2. **Is `t` evaluated per line item or per invoice total?** Slide 5 says the acceptance limit applies
   to "the same line item", which implies per item — but the completeness strategy in §7 lives or
   dies on this. **[?]**
3. **Net or gross?** The sample invoice shows Net / plus VAT / Total amount. Bidding on the wrong one
   is a ~19% error, larger than most teams' margin. **[?]**
4. **How do we submit?** An API, or a web form a human types into? If it is a form, "plays cleanly
   for many rounds" becomes a browser-automation problem and role 1 changes completely. **[?]**
5. **What does the Transactions tab actually return?** Rich per-bid data, or only payment totals?
   This decides whether role 4 parses opponents' bids directly or reverse-engineers bounds. **[?]**
6. **How many rounds, and over what window?** Determines how much the calibration loop can learn and
   whether overnight coverage is needed. **[?]**

---

## 12. Known discrepancies between sources

The deck predates the challenge page; where they disagree, trust the page.

| Detail | Slides | Challenge page |
|---|---|---|
| Round cadence | every 10 minutes | **every 15 minutes** |
| Invoice | slide 5 shows a pre-filled invoice | **blank invoice**, we author the line items |
| Title | "Claim to Fame" | **"Insurance Invoice Poker"** |

The blank-invoice difference is the significant one: it turns the task from auditing someone else's
invoice into composing our own, which is what makes the completeness lever in §7 available at all.

- Decline at `b` = 600 and eat a penalty → **`t` > 600** (an expensive way to learn it)

After a few rounds on similar line items, the fair rate for "lay laminate, per m²" is squeezed into
a tight interval that nobody ever told us.

The same logic reads opponents: if Team X paid our €690 bill, then **`b_X` ≥ 690**. Tracked across
rounds, that tells us who is loose and who is tight, and therefore how high `a` can safely go.

**Probing asymmetry [I]:** probe with `a`, not `b`. A rejected invoice just earns nothing that
round. A wrong decline costs payout plus penalty. So be adventurous on the pricing side and
conservative on the acceptance side until the data is in.

---

## 7. Strategy

### The central claim

The penalty rule forces every rational team to keep `b` at or just above their own estimate of `t`,
because sitting below it is actively punished. If everyone's `b` hovers near fair value, then `a`
just under `t` gets paid by almost everyone. **The game therefore collapses to estimating `t`
accurately.** Opponent modelling is a real but second-order edge.

### The lever most teams will miss [I]

The invoice arrives **blank** — we author the line items — and the acceptance limit is defined per
**line item**, not per invoice total.

If that holds, adding a *legitimate* line item that other teams forget is nearly free revenue.
Water damage to a floor is not only "remove laminate, lay laminate": there is debris disposal,
furniture moving, drying-equipment rental, skirting boards. Each is judged separately against fair
value, so a **complete** invoice earns more than a **padded** one, without ever crossing into fraud.

Most teams will tune unit prices and never touch invoice completeness.

**This must be verified before we build on it.** If rejection turns out to be per invoice rather
than per line item, adding items becomes a risk instead of an edge. See open question 2.

### Consistency is an engineering problem, not a modelling one

The judging criteria include *"Consistency: the more rounds it plays cleanly, the better."* A bot
that plays every round through the night beats a smarter one that someone forgets to run at 03:00.
Build for unattended uptime: retries, timeouts, and a safe fallback bid on any failure path.

---

## 8. Architecture

```
fetch round → parse policy + damage report → build line items
           → estimate fair value per item (+ confidence interval)
           → a = t̂_low · (1 − margin),  b = t̂_high · (1 + margin)
           → submit → ingest public results → recalibrate
```

Stages:

1. **Ingest** — fetch the round's policy, damage report, and blank invoice.
2. **Understand** — extract damage type, affected areas, quantities, and the policy's coverage,
   deductible, and limits into a structured claim object.
3. **Compose** — build the line items, aiming for completeness against the damage described.
4. **Price** — quantity × unit rate from a German trade-rate knowledge base, producing a fair-value
   estimate and a confidence interval per line.
5. **Bid** — derive `a` and `b` from the interval, with the margin driven by confidence and by the
   penalty asymmetry.
6. **Submit** — inside the one-minute window, with a fallback bid if anything upstream fails.
7. **Learn** — ingest public results, tighten the rate intervals, and update per-opponent limit
   estimates.

Step 7 is the differentiator. It also answers two judged criteria directly: *"Generality: also works
on completely new policies"* and *"Approach: the strategy you went in with, and how it changed as
you played."*

---

**What you built:**

- **Score** — Where you finished. The main signal, not the only one
- **Generality** — Also works on completely new policies
- **Consistency** — The more rounds it plays cleanly, the better

**How you pitch it:**

- **Clarity** — If we can't follow it, we can't credit it
- **Problem** — What's hard about pricing a claim from both sides
- **Approach** — The strategy you went in with, and how it changed as you played
- **Solution** — What you ended up with, and the logic behind it

| Who | Owns |
|---|---|
| 1 | Platform integration, round loop, submission reliability |
| 2 | Policy and damage-report parsing → structured claim |
| 3 | German trade-rate knowledge base + fair-value estimator |
| 4 | Results ingestion, calibration, opponent modelling |
| 5 | Pitch deck, live demo, README and repo hygiene |

6. **How many rounds, and over what window?** Determines how much the calibration loop can learn and

# 🏆 Claim to Fame

Hello hackers, welcome to QuantCo's _Claim to Fame_ challenge!

---

## 🎭 Scenario

In insurances, a _claim_ is a request by a policyholder asking for payment or financial compensation. After property damage or a car accident, tradespeople such as handymen and repair garages issue invoices. Policyholders submit these invoices to their insurance providers, which decide whether to pay.

But not everyone is honest, so for each invoiced item the insurer must judge whether it is:

- **Covered** by the policy,
- **Related** to the reported damage, and
- **Reasonably** priced (we refer to "total" price per line item in this challenge = quantity * unit price)

A fraudulent claim fails one of these: it isn't insured, the item is unrelated to the case, or the price is inflated.

## 🎯 Your Task

In this challenge you're competing against other teams in rounds. Your goal is to **a) maximize the amount of money you make** and **b) do so with style**.

In this challenge, you will take on two roles simultaneously:

| Role                             | What you do                                                                                                                                                    |
| -------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 🧾 **Invoice Issuer (Handyman)** | Set the price (= quantity * unit price) for each line item on the invoice that you think you're entitled to. If you set a fair price, you will get your money! |
| 🔍 **Insurance Claim Handling**  | Review incoming invoices and minimize the amount your team pays. Spot fraudulent items and set a maximum fair price above which you reject payments.           |

In every round, you submit the prices a and b for all items, your submissions will be matched against all other teams.

> ⚠️ **But bear in mind:** you can't charge or pay whatever you like. There is a **fair value threshold `t`** for each item. If you reject a request that was at or below this value, you will get a penalty.

## 🎲 The Game

In regular intervals, a case will be released. You then have _exactly one minute_ to submit. Once the case is released, you will be able to fetch a _decryption key_ from the API. This can then be used to decrypt the `.zip` file for the case. Each case consists of:

| File              | Contents                                            |
| ----------------- | --------------------------------------------------- |
| `policy.txt`      | An **insurance policy** describing what is covered  |
| `description.txt` | A **damage description** explaining the claim       |
| `invoices.pdf`    | An **invoice** containing line items without prices |
| `images.png`      | Some cases might also contain **images**            |

After decrypting and extracting, you should analyze the files and set two values for every line item:

- **Charge price (`a`)**: the amount you charge opposing teams. _Default: `0`_
- **Acceptance limit (`b`)**: the maximum amount your team is willing to accept and pay when receiving the same line item from another team. _Default: `0`_

> 💶 **Always submit the _gross total_.** Both the charge price `a` and the acceptance limit `b` must always be given as the gross total for the whole line item. Never the net amount, and never a per-unit price.

As mentioned, there will be a **secret threshold (`t`) representing the maximum price that a claims expert would consider appropriate**. For line items that are **not covered** by the policy: `t = 0`.

### 💸 Payoffs

In the following: `H` is the handyman who issues the invoice, `I` is the insurance that does the claim handling and invoice checking.

Everything hinges on where the charge price `a` falls relative to the secret threshold `t`. Picture it on a number line:

```
        fair zone  (a ≤ t)         │      fraud zone  (a > t)
  ◀────────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────▶
  0                                t                                 a →
  the price is valid; H is owed it │ the price is inflated; H is not owed it
```

- **Left of `t`, the fair zone (`a ≤ t`).** The charge is legitimate, so `H` is entitled to the money. `I` _should_ accept: accepting pays the fair `a`, while rejecting still owes `H` the `a` **plus** a `0.5a` lawyer penalty on `I`.
- **Right of `t`, the fraud zone (`a > t`).** The charge is inflated, so `H` is not owed anything. `I` _should_ reject: rejecting means no money flows, while accepting hands `H` the fraudulent amount.

The threshold `t` is the dividing line between the two, and it's secret; both roles are really betting on which side of `t` each price sits.

> 🧢 **Accepted-payment cap.** Each line item has a secret payment cap c, shared across all teams, where `c ≥ 4t` (and never below an absolute floor). If a charge is accepted, the insurer pays and the issuer receives min(a,c). This prevents teams from winning through a single exorbitantly high charge.

The table below details what happens for each transaction.

|                            | `a ≤ t`: price okay               | `a > t`: price fraudulent                  |
| -------------------------- | --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| **`a ≤ b` price accepted** | `I` pays `a`, `H` gets `a`        | `I` pays `min(a, c)`, `H` gets `min(a, c)` |
| **`a > b` price rejected** | `I` pays `a + 0.5a`, `H` gets `a` | `I` pays `0`, `H` gets `0`                 |

**Left column (`a ≤ t`): the price is valid.**

- If insurance `I` accepts (`a ≤ b`), it pays the claim: `I` pays `a`, `H` gets `a`.
- If insurance `I` wrongfully rejects (`a > b`), `H` still gets the `a` it is owed, but `I` also pays a lawyer as a penalty `0.5a`, so `I` pays `1.5a` in total.

**Right column (`a > t`): the price is fraudulent.**

- If insurance `I` accepts (`a ≤ b`), `H` is in luck and pockets the capped fraudulent amount `min(a, c)`.
- If insurance `I` rightfully rejects (`a > b`), no money flows.

## 🧮 An example round

Let's walk through a single round with three teams (**Alpha Squad**, **Beta Dynamics**, and **Delta Strategies**) and just **one line item**: a replacement windshield. Suppose the secret fair value threshold for this item is `t = 100`.

The game starts at 19:00:00. Teams then have exactly one minute to fetch the decryption key, decrypt the zip file, analyze it and submit they charge price `a` and acceptance limit `b`.
Suppose the teams submit:

| Team             | Charge `a` | Acceptance limit `b` |
| ---------------- | ---------- | -------------------- |
| Alpha Squad      | `100`      | `130`                |
| Beta Dynamics    | `150`      | `90`                 |
| Delta Strategies | `100`      | `110`                |

Every team is matched against every other team, in both roles. For each matchup, the **issuer** acts as the handyman `H` (charging its `a`) and the **reviewer** acts as the insurance `I` (deciding with its `b`). That gives six transactions:

| Issuer (H) → Reviewer (I) | `a`   | Reviewer's `b` | `a ≤ t`? | `a ≤ b`?  | Outcome                                                   |
| ------------------------- | ----- | -------------- | -------- | --------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| Alpha → Beta              | `100` | `90`           | ✅ okay  | ❌ reject | Wrongful reject: Beta pays `1.5a = 150`, Alpha gets `100` |
| Alpha → Delta             | `100` | `110`          | ✅ okay  | ✅ accept | Delta pays `100`, Alpha gets `100`                        |
| Delta → Alpha             | `100` | `130`          | ✅ okay  | ✅ accept | Alpha pays `100`, Delta gets `100`                        |
| Delta → Beta              | `100` | `90`           | ✅ okay  | ❌ reject | Wrongful reject: Beta pays `1.5a = 150`, Delta gets `100` |
| Beta → Alpha              | `150` | `130`          | ❌ fraud | ❌ reject | Rightful reject: no money flows                           |
| Beta → Delta              | `150` | `110`          | ❌ fraud | ❌ reject | Rightful reject: no money flows                           |

Adding up what each team **gets** (as customer) minus what it **pays** (as insurance):

| Team             | Gets  | Pays  | **Net**    |
| ---------------- | ----- | ----- | ---------- |
| Alpha Squad      | `200` | `100` | **`+100`** |
| Delta Strategies | `200` | `100` | **`+100`** |
| Beta Dynamics    | `0`   | `300` | **`−300`** |

The lesson: **Beta Dynamics loses on both sides.** As a customer it overcharged (`a = 150 > t`), so its fraudulent claims were rightfully rejected and it earned nothing. As an insurance it set its acceptance limit too low (`b = 90 < t`), so it wrongfully rejected fair claims and paid the `1.5a` lawyer penalty + compensation twice. Alpha and Delta both charged fairly and set acceptance limits above the threshold, so they collected their money and avoided penalties.

## ⚙️ Game Setup

To participate, you need to take multiple steps.

### 1. Register

First, register for the challenge. To do so, come up to us, tell us your team and Discord username to obtain your API key. Details will follow on Discord.

You will then obtain your key. This key is unique and unchangeable. **Do not share it** with anyone outside your team (duh), as they would be able to trade on your behalf.

### 2. Get the Cases

Later, we will provide a link to a folder. The folder will contain a number of encrypted `.zip` files, one for each case. There is a test case (case 0) in the folder. Together with the provided `starter_script.py`, you can use the endpoint to see if your requests are properly formatted. The endpoint accepts any well-formatted JSON. Further details can be found in [API_HANDBOOK.md](API_HANDBOOK.md) in the folder.

## 🚫 Fair play

This is a competition between teams, so anything that undermines that is off limits. This includes:

- **No cross-team collaboration.** Do not coordinate prices, acceptance limits, or strategies with other teams, and do not share your analysis of a case with them.
- **No sharing keys or credentials.** Your API key belongs to your team only. Never submit on behalf of another team, and never let another team submit on yours.
- **No attacking the platform.** Do not try to obtain decryption keys before a case is released, read other teams' submissions, extract the secret thresholds, or otherwise probe, overload, or exploit the API and its infrastructure.
- **Anything inside your own team is fair game.** Build tooling, use LLMs, do stuff manually, research the domain, ...

> ⚠️ Cheating gets your team disqualified from the tournament. If you are unsure whether something is allowed, just ask the organizers.

## 🥇 How to win

Shortly before the challenge ends, you are asked to provide a small write-up of your strategy. We will assess your approach and look at how well it performed to determine the winner. The best teams will present their approach to us.

## 🧰 What you need

Inside the shared folder, we include a starter script in Python to get you going, but you can use any language, library, or framework you'd like. The `starter_script.py` that already implements this flow for the mentioned test `Case 0`. Run it to get an idea of how things work.

To run it, you'll need to provide your API keys (`TEAM_API_KEY` and `OPENAI_KEY`) as environment variables — the script prompts you for the team API key if `TEAM_API_KEY` is not set — and install its dependencies: the Python packages `requests` and `openai`, plus **7-Zip**, which the script calls to decrypt the case archives.

**The easy way ([Pixi](https://pixi.sh)):** we ship a `pixi.toml` that pulls in Python, both packages, and 7-Zip in one go. From this folder just run:

```bash
pixi install
pixi run python starter_script.py
```

**The manual way:** in a plain Python environment, install the packages with `pip install requests openai`, then install 7-Zip so that the `7z` command is on your `PATH`:

- **macOS** (via [Homebrew](https://brew.sh)): `brew install p7zip`
- **Linux (Debian/Ubuntu):** `sudo apt install p7zip-full`
- **Windows:** download and run the installer from [7-zip.org/download.html](https://www.7-zip.org/download.html), then add the install folder (e.g. `C:\Program Files\7-Zip`) to your `PATH` so the `7z` command works from the terminal.

It makes sense to decide on one person to actually run and submit the script. **Later submissions overwrite earlier ones.** Also think about how you will schedule future runs, as new challenges might run throughout the entire tournament.

## 🚀 OOOOOKAY, let's goo

To check upcoming games, your progress and the leaderboard, visit **https://c2f.public.quantco.cloud/leaderboard/**.

# Insurance Invoice Poker — QuantCo challenge brief

Team Bayern CodeWerk · EHL Munich (match 3) · 22–23 August 2026

Our working reference for the challenge. **[C]** = confirmed from source, **[I]** = our reasoning,
**[?]** = still unverified.

**Source of truth: [`GAME_DESCRIPTION.md`](GAME_DESCRIPTION.md)** — the official handout, in this
repo. Where it disagrees with the slide deck or the EHL challenge page, it wins. See §12.

Secondary sources: `~/Downloads/QuantCo Claim-to-Fame slides.pdf` (opening-ceremony deck), the EHL
challenge-selection page, and `API_HANDBOOK.md` in the shared case folder (we do not have this yet).

---

## 1. At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Official title | **Insurance Invoice Poker** / "Claim to Fame", by QuantCo |
| Format | Every team matched against every other team, both roles, every round |
| Decision window | **Exactly one minute** from case release to submission |
| Submitted per line item | Charge price `a` and acceptance limit `b`, both **gross totals** |
| Wrongful-reject penalty | `0.5a` lawyer fee on top of the `a` still owed |
| Payment cap | Secret `c ≥ 4t`, shared across teams |
| Leaderboard | https://c2f.public.quantco.cloud/leaderboard/ |
| Prize | €1000, plus AirPods Pro 3 + €100 coding-agent credit per person |
| Deliverables | Pitch deck · GitHub repo · live demo · **strategy write-up before the end** |

Goal, verbatim: *"maximize the amount of money you make"* and *"do so with style"*.

---

## 2. The scenario

A **claim** is a policyholder asking their insurer to pay. Tradespeople issue invoices after damage;
the policyholder submits them; the insurer decides whether to pay. For each invoiced line item the
insurer must judge whether it is **[C]**:

- **Covered** by the policy,
- **Related** to the reported damage, and
- **Reasonably** priced — where price means the *total* for the line item, i.e. quantity × unit price.

A fraudulent item fails one of these three. Note that only the third is a pricing question — the
other two are document comprehension, and they are where the asymmetry lives (§7).

---

## 3. Roles and mechanics

Each round you play both roles simultaneously **[C]**:

| Role | What you do |
|---|---|
| 🧾 **Invoice Issuer (Handyman)** | Set the price for each line item you think you're entitled to |
| 🔍 **Insurance Claim Handling** | Set a maximum fair price above which you reject incoming items |

Every line item has a **secret threshold `t`** — the maximum a claims expert would consider
appropriate. **For line items not covered by the policy, `t = 0`.** **[C]**

You submit two numbers per line item, both as the **gross total for the whole line item** — never
net, never per-unit **[C]**:

- **`a`** — charge price, what you bill opposing teams. Default `0`.
- **`b`** — acceptance limit, the most you'll pay for that same item from another team. Default `0`.

### The payoff table [C]

`H` is the handyman issuing the invoice, `I` the insurance reviewing it.

| | `a ≤ t`: price okay | `a > t`: price fraudulent |
|---|---|---|
| **`a ≤ b`: accepted** | `I` pays `a`, `H` gets `a` | `I` pays `min(a,c)`, `H` gets `min(a,c)` |
| **`a > b`: rejected** | `I` pays `a + 0.5a`, `H` gets `a` | `I` pays `0`, `H` gets `0` |

**Accepted-payment cap:** each item has a secret cap `c ≥ 4t`, shared across all teams. An accepted
charge pays `min(a, c)`, which stops anyone winning on one absurd charge. **[C]**

---

## 4. The round loop [C]

1. A case is released at a fixed time.
2. Fetch a **decryption key** from the API.
3. Decrypt the case `.zip` (7-Zip).
4. Analyse the contents and submit `a` and `b` for every line item — **within one minute**.

Case contents:

| File | Contents |
|---|---|
| `policy.txt` | The insurance policy, describing what is covered |
| `description.txt` | The damage description explaining the claim |
| `invoices.pdf` | The invoice, **line items without prices** |
| `images.png` | Some cases also include images |

**Later submissions overwrite earlier ones.** So submit a safe bid immediately on decrypt, then
refine it until the window closes. That converts the one-minute deadline from a hard cliff into a
soft one, and it is free insurance against a slow model call. **[I]**

---

## 5. The official worked example [C]

One line item — a replacement windshield — with secret threshold `t = 100`. Three teams submit:

| Team | Charge `a` | Acceptance limit `b` |
|---|---|---|
| Alpha Squad | 100 | 130 |
| Beta Dynamics | 150 | 90 |
| Delta Strategies | 100 | 110 |

Everyone is matched against everyone in both roles — six transactions:

| Issuer → Reviewer | `a` | their `b` | `a ≤ t`? | `a ≤ b`? | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Alpha → Beta | 100 | 90 | ✅ | ❌ | Wrongful reject: Beta pays 150, Alpha gets 100 |
| Alpha → Delta | 100 | 110 | ✅ | ✅ | Delta pays 100, Alpha gets 100 |
| Delta → Alpha | 100 | 130 | ✅ | ✅ | Alpha pays 100, Delta gets 100 |
| Delta → Beta | 100 | 90 | ✅ | ❌ | Wrongful reject: Beta pays 150, Delta gets 100 |
| Beta → Alpha | 150 | 130 | ❌ | ❌ | Rightful reject: no money flows |
| Beta → Delta | 150 | 110 | ❌ | ❌ | Rightful reject: no money flows |

| Team | Gets | Pays | **Net** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Alpha Squad | 200 | 100 | **+100** |
| Delta Strategies | 200 | 100 | **+100** |
| Beta Dynamics | 0 | 300 | **−300** |

Beta lost on both sides at once: it overcharged (`150 > t`) so earned nothing, and set `b = 90 < t`
so it wrongfully rejected two fair claims and paid the lawyer fee twice.

---

## 6. The strategy, derived

### `a` and `b` are independent decisions [I]

`a` determines what we earn. `b` determines what we pay. Neither feeds the other. Optimise them
separately, from one shared belief about `t`.

### Opponents' limits do not affect our income

Read the left column of the payoff table again: when `a ≤ t`, **`H` gets `a` whether the reviewer
accepts or rejects.** A wrongful rejection costs the *rejecter* an extra `0.5a`; it costs us nothing.

So as long as we price under `t`, our revenue is completely independent of every opponent's `b`.
Opponent modelling buys us nothing on the issuing side. **[I]**

### Optimal `b`: accept only above 2/3 confidence

Facing a charge `a`, with `p` = our confidence that `a ≤ t`, and assuming `a ≤ c`:

- **Accept** → we pay `a` if fair, `min(a,c) = a` if fraud. Expected cost = **`a`**.
- **Reject** → we pay `1.5a` if fair, `0` if fraud. Expected cost = **`1.5pa`**.

Rejecting is better when `1.5pa < a`, i.e. when `p < 2/3`.

> **Accept only if more than 2/3 confident the price is fair.**
> Equivalently: set `b` at the **33rd percentile** of our posterior over `t`.

A wrong rejection only costs `0.5a` extra; a wrong acceptance costs the full amount. Being somewhat
trigger-happy is correct — `b` belongs *below* our best guess of `t`, not above it. **[I]**

### Optimal `a`: maximise `a · P(t ≥ a)`

Assuming opponents rightfully reject fraud, expected revenue is `a` times the probability the charge
is fair. Maximise numerically over a grid.

For a lognormal belief with median `m` and log-sd `σ`, the optimum solves `σ·Φ(−u) = φ(u)`:

| `σ` (uncertainty) | optimal `a` | implied acceptance rate | optimal `b` |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.2 | `0.78 · m` | ~90% | `0.92 · m` |
| 0.3 | `0.75 · m` | ~83% | `0.88 · m` |

Two things to notice. **Charge roughly 75–80% of your median estimate** — the optimum is far more
conservative than instinct suggests, because crossing `t` costs the entire line. And `a < b` in both
rows, which is the sanity check: we would accept our own invoice. **[I]**

Uncertainty is expensive in both directions. Every point of accuracy in the estimator moves `a` up
and `b` up together, which is the whole game.

### Where opponents *do* matter: the fraud gamble [I]

Charging `a > t` pays `min(a, c)` when accepted and `0` when rejected, with `c ≥ 4t`. Charging `4t`
beats charging `t` only if more than ~25% of teams would accept it. That is measurable from public
results, but it is a side bet with a high variance and it is not the core game. **Park it.** Revisit
only if the leaderboard shows a large bloc of loose acceptance limits.

---

## 7. Where the money actually is: `t = 0` [I]

For anything the policy does not cover, the threshold is zero. That means:

- **As issuer:** any `a > 0` on an uncovered item is automatically fraud. Guaranteed zero, and the
  correct charge is exactly `0`.
- **As insurer:** `b` must be `0` on those items, or we pay for someone else's fraud in full.

This is a binary, and it is decided by reading `policy.txt` against `description.txt` — not by
estimating a price. Getting it right is worth more than a good rate table, because the pricing error
on a normal item is a percentage while the error here is the entire line. Teams that skim the policy
will bleed on exactly these items.

The same logic applies to the **related** test: an item that is real and covered but unconnected to
the described damage is also fraud.

**Priority order for the pipeline: coverage → relatedness → price.** The first two are classification
problems with huge payoffs; the third is a regression problem with modest ones.

---

## 8. Architecture

```
fetch key → decrypt zip → parse policy + description + invoice (+ images)
          → per line item:  covered?  related?   →  t = 0 if either fails
                            else estimate t̂ with an uncertainty band
          → a = argmax a·P(t ≥ a)      b = 33rd percentile of t̂
          → submit immediately, then refine until the window closes
          → ingest public results → recalibrate the rate table
```

1. **Ingest** — poll for release, fetch key, decrypt, extract.
2. **Parse** — `policy.txt`, `description.txt`, `invoices.pdf` line items, any images.
3. **Screen** — coverage and relatedness per line item. Fail either → `a = b = 0`.
4. **Price** — quantity × unit rate from a German trade-rate knowledge base, as a distribution, not

the policyholder submits them; the insurer decides whether to pay. For each invoiced line item the
insurer must judge whether it is **[C]**:

- **Covered** by the policy,
- **Related** to the reported damage, and
- **Reasonably** priced — where price means the *total* for the line item, i.e. quantity × unit price.

other two are document comprehension, and they are where the asymmetry lives (§7).

---

Each round you play both roles simultaneously **[C]**:

| Role | What you do |
|---|---|
| 🧾 **Invoice Issuer (Handyman)** | Set the price for each line item you think you're entitled to |
| 🔍 **Insurance Claim Handling** | Set a maximum fair price above which you reject incoming items |

Here's the concrete version. One line item — a windshield — secret threshold **`t` = 100**, cap **`c` = 400** (since `c ≥ 4t`). Say there are **10 opponents**, and they split into two camps:

- **5 tight teams** with `b` = 90
- **5 loose teams** with `b` = 150

## Case 1: we price fairly, `a` = 100

| Opponent type | Their `b` | Accept? | They pay | **We get** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 5 tight | 90 | ❌ reject | 150 each (`1.5a`) | **100 each** |
| 5 loose | 150 | ✅ accept | 100 each | **100 each** |

**Our income = 1000.** Identical from both camps.

The tight teams rejected us and it made no difference to us at all — they just paid an extra 50 each for the privilege. Knowing in advance that half the field would reject us would not have changed our bid by a single euro.

**This is the normal case, and opponents are irrelevant in it.**

## Case 2: we gamble, `a` = 400

Now we're deliberately in the fraud zone (`400 > t = 100`), hoping someone's limit is loose enough.

| Opponent type | Their `b` | Accept? | **We get** |
|---|---|---|---|
| 5 tight | 90 | ❌ | **0** |
| 5 loose | 150 | ❌ | **0** |

**Our income = 0.** We just lost the 1000 we'd have banked by playing fair, because nobody's limit reached 400.

Now change one thing — suppose 3 of the 10 teams had `b` = 500:

| Count | Their `b` | Accept? | **We get** |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3 | 500 | ✅ | **400 each = 1200** |
| 7 | < 400 | ❌ | 0 |

**Income = 1200 > 1000.** The gamble wins.

### The break-even

`n` teams accepting at the cap must beat 10 teams paying fair value:

```
n × 400  >  10 × 100     →     n > 2.5
```

So the gamble pays only if **more than 25% of the field has `b` ≥ 4t**. That ratio is `c/t = 4`, so the rule generalises: you need better than **1-in-4** acceptance.

**That single number — what fraction of teams have wildly loose limits — is the only thing about other teams that can ever change our bid.** And it's estimable from the public results: watch for teams paying out on items that later prove to be far above fair value.

## Why we still can't profile individual teams

Even if we knew Beta Dynamics was a chronic overcharger and Delta Strategies was careful, we couldn't act on it. We submit **one `b` per line item, matched against all teams**. There's no per-opponent limit. So a profile of any individual team is unusable information.

## The one genuinely useful thing

Other teams' *past* bids are free data about **`t` itself**, not about them.

If eight teams charged 95–105 for a windshield last round and those charges were accepted, then `t ≥ 105` and eight independent estimators converged near 100. That's a much better read on the market rate than our own estimate alone.

But notice what that is: we're using opponents as **sensors for `t`**, not as adversaries to outwit. It feeds the rate table, not a game-theory module.

## What this means for the build

Don't build an opponent-modelling component. Build the `t` estimator, and pipe public results back into it. Role 4 in the work split already says exactly that — *"price estimation with uncertainty, plus recalibration from public results."*

Track the loose-team fraction as a single logged number so we *could* take the gamble late in the tournament if the leaderboard shows the field is soft. Don't design around it.
